newsitem.title: USA: Visa, MasterCard begin tests of smart-cards.
newsitem.headline: Visa, MasterCard begin tests of smart-cards.

text.p: Major U.S. financial institutions are launching smart-card tests, taking baby steps closer to bringing the long-awaited technology to your home PC, bank ATM machine or subway turnstile.

During a six-month trial that begins this summer, several hundred San Francisco employees of Visa and Bank of America will use so-called "stored value" smart cards on the Internet to buy software, greeting cards and financial newsletters. But whatever the outcome, Bank of America officials don't expect a mass-market roll out for another three to five years.

Earlier this month, an international consortium led by MasterCard introduced a secure, open smart-card operating system the group claims will enable one smart card to work many ways, for example, as a credit card, debit card, frequent flyer mileage card, subway pass and video store I.D. MasterCard expects to have the first of these multi-purpose cards to banks in early 1998.
Electronic commerce experts believe smart cards will be a recognised electronic payment option by the turn of the century and possibly overtake other forms of online payments.
Even before then, they see it becoming a favoured Internet and corporate intranet security device.

Smart cards are plastic cards with an embedded microprocessor that can store information or monetary value or both. Today's smart cards generally use an 8-bit microprocessor and hold one kilobyte to eight kilobytes of data. That's enough to store several pages of text, or run a small software application.
By comparison, the magnetic stripe on the back of a credit card holds about 50 characters, enough for a bank PIN number but little else.

Expectations for smart cards are great. Jupiter Communications, the New York interactive services researcher, predicts that by the end of 1998, smart cards will account for about 10 percent of all online purchases, growing to 26 percent by 2000.

But advances won't come without significant breakthroughs, including convincing banks to issue cards, and retailers and consumer to buy hardware needed to use them. Prices for producing cards, which now run around $9 each, also have to drop.

"It's going to take a company with the scope and breadth of a MasterCard or Visa to move this forward," said Harry Zenick, an analyst with Zona Research in Redwood City, Calif. As for consumers leading the way, "it won't happen," he said.

Smart cards have been common abroad for some time. Of 100 million smart cards expected to be used this year, 95 percent of them will be in Europe, according to American Banker, the banking industry newspaper. Card use here has been stymied by America's love affair with credit cards and a strong ATM system, said David Jung, an analyst with Killen & Associates, in Palo Alto, Calif.
But in recent months, smart-card partnerships and pilot projects are popping up everywhere.
"You're seeing smart cards move out of the laboratories and into public trials," said David Weisman, finance analyst with Forrester Research in Cambridge, Mass.

Activity is focused in two areas, security and payments. Companies are developing secure smart cards that double as identification for employees, suppliers and customers using corporate intranets and extranets.

But a standards battle is brewing, with Microsoft, France's Bull, Hewlett-Packard, Schlumberger and others lining up behind one set of smart-card specs, and IBM, Netscape, Oracle and Sun Microsystems favouring the Java-based OpenCard Framework standard.

Farther behind is the use of smart cards in lieu of cash. This spring, AT&T and Mondex -- in which MasterCard holds a 51 percent stake -- teamed up on a smart-card micropayment system for the Web. The partners will test it this year before deploying it in 1999.

Chip-maker Motorola created a smart-card division and plans to ship products by the fourth quarter. Hewlett-Packard is testing smart cards for Web payments with a German bank and a number of unnamed retailers, and is offering smart-card hardware-and-software packages for corporations.
General Electric Co.'s GE Capital division, GTE, General Motors and American Express also are eyeing the market.
One of the biggest trials of multi-use smart cards is at Florida State University, where 35,000 students and faculty use smart cards in vending machines, laundries, bookstores and cafeterias.

In another experiment, 11,000 Ohio residents use smart cards loaded with electronic food stamps at 95 retailers in the Dayton area. The programme is expected to expand statewide by 2000, with 450,000 cards and 7,000 retailers.
At home or work, experts believe people will swipe cards through a reader built into their computer keyboard or CPU.

One company has developed a reader that fits inside a PC's 3.5-inch floppy drive. Fischer International in Naples, Fla., sells a $60 retrofit reader called the "Smarty" that will be used in trials later this year conducted by MasterCard, Citibank and Chase Manhattan, and in pilot tests at BankAmerica and Wells Fargo.
(Michelle V. Rafter writes about cyberspace and technology from Los Angeles. Reach her at mvrafter(at)deltanet.com. Opinions expressed in this column are her own).
